claim: Cortico-basal ganglia circuits are thought to mediate goal-directed learning by a process of outcome evaluation to gradually select appropriate motor actions.
source: Cortico-basal ganglia circuits are thought to mediate goal-directed learning by a process of outcome evaluation to gradually select appropriate motor actions.
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific understanding in the field, drawing from general knowledge about cortico-basal ganglia function.

claim: Spiking patterns of single neurons in both core and shell subregions during singing correlated with acoustic similarity to tutor syllables.
source: Spiking patterns of single neurons in both core and shell subregions during singing correlated with acoustic similarity to tutor syllables, suggesting a process of outcome evaluation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing correlations between neural activity and tutor similarity.

claim: Both core and shell neurons encoded tutor similarity via either increases or decreases in firing rate.
source: Both core and shell neurons encoded tutor similarity via either increases or decreases in firing rate, although only shell neurons showed a significant association at the population level.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data showing both positive and negative correlations between firing rate and tutor similarity.

claim: Only shell neurons showed a significant association between firing rate and tutor similarity at the population level.
source: Both core and shell neurons encoded tutor similarity via either increases or decreases in firing rate, although only shell neurons showed a significant association at the population level.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of population-level data using mixed-effects linear regression.

claim: Tutor similarity predicted firing rates most strongly during early stages of learning.
source: Tutor similarity predicted firing rates most strongly during early stages of learning, and shell but not core neurons showed decreases in response variability across development, suggesting that the activity of shell neurons reflects the progression of learning.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses showing stronger associations between firing rate and tutor similarity during early development.

claim: Shell but not core neurons showed decreases in response variability across development.
source: Tutor similarity predicted firing rates most strongly during early stages of learning, and shell but not core neurons showed decreases in response variability across development, suggesting that the activity of shell neurons reflects the progression of learning.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of coefficient of variation (CV) of firing rates across development.

claim: The activity of shell neurons reflects the progression of learning.
source: Tutor similarity predicted firing rates most strongly during early stages of learning, and shell but not core neurons showed decreases in response variability across development, suggesting that the activity of shell neurons reflects the progression of learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental changes in shell neuron activity patterns that parallel behavioral learning.

claim: Juvenile songbirds memorize vocal sounds of an adult tutor.
source: Similar to infants learning speech, juvenile songbirds memorize vocal sounds of an adult tutor.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of songbird vocal learning.

claim: Juvenile songbirds progressively refine their own vocal behavior to imitate the tutor song through iterative comparisons between feedback of their own vocalizations and tutor sounds.
source: They then progressively refine their own vocal behavior to imitate the tutor song through iterative comparisons between feedback of their own vocalizations and tutor sounds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the songbird vocal learning process.

claim: Successful acquisition of song requires the evaluation of behavioral feedback against a representation of the goal (tutor song) to guide the gradual acquisition of an accurate imitation during the sensorimotor stage of vocal learning.
source: Successful acquisition requires the evaluation of behavioral feedback against a representation of the goal (tutor song) to guide the gradual acquisition of an accurate imitation during the sensorimotor stage of vocal learning.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of the vocal learning process in songbirds.

claim: Neural control of vocal learning in juvenile zebra finches is vested in cortico-basal ganglia loops that emanate from the cortical nucleus LMAN.
source: Neural control of vocal learning in juvenile zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) is vested in cortico-basal ganglia loops that emanate from the cortical nucleus LMAN (lateral magnocellular nucleus of the anterior nidopallium; Figure 1) (Aronov et al., 2008; Bottjer et al., 1984; Scharff and Nottebohm, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research establishing the role of LMAN in vocal learning.

claim: Core and surrounding shell subregions of LMAN make parallel connections through the basal ganglia and thalamus.
source: Core and surrounding shell subregions of LMAN make parallel connections through the basal ganglia and thalamus (Bottjer, 2004; Luo et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 1995; Gale et al., 2008; Person et al., 2008; Iyengar et al., 1999; Paterson and Bottjer, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Core and shell subregions of LMAN appear functionally similar to sensorimotor and associative cortico-basal ganglia loops that contribute to different aspects of motor learning in mammals.
source: and appear functionally similar to sensorimotor and associative cortico-basal ganglia loops that contribute to different aspects of motor learning in mammals (Thorn et al., 2010; Yin et al., 2008; Samejima and Doya, 2007; Ashby et al., 2010; Redgrave et al., 2010; Graybiel, 2008; Gremel and Costa, 2013; Yin et al., 2009; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Alexander and Crutcher, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of mammalian cortico-basal ganglia circuits.

claim: The core pathway mediates vocal motor production in juvenile songbirds.
source: The core pathway mediates vocal motor production in juvenile songbirds (Elliott et al., 2014; Scharff and Nottebohm, 1991; Aronov et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on the function of the core pathway.

claim: Lesions in the shell pathway of juvenile birds impair the ability to copy tutor song syllables, but do not cause motor disruption of song.
source: whereas the shell pathway is involved in evaluating sensorimotor learning; lesions in the shell pathway of juvenile birds impair the ability to copy tutor song syllables, but do not cause motor disruption of song (Bottjer and Altenau, 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a lesion study and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The disruption of learning but not motor performance by shell pathway lesions supports the idea that shell circuitry helps to evaluate whether self-generated vocalizations match learned tutor sounds.
source: This disruption of learning, but not motor performance, supports the idea that shell circuitry helps to evaluate whether self-generated vocalizations match learned tutor sounds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lesion data showing selective impairment of learning.

claim: Within the shell subregion of LMAN in juvenile birds, distinct subpopulations of neurons respond selectively to playback of either their learned tutor song or their own self-generated song.
source: Within the shell subregion of LMAN in juvenile birds, distinct subpopulations of neurons respond selectively to playback of either their learned tutor song or their own self-generated song (Achiro and Bottjer, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The shell pathway has access to neural representations of the goal behavior and the current version of the bird's own song.
source: indicating that the shell pathway has access to neural representations of the goal behavior and the current version of the bird's own song (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of neurons tuned to tutor song and own song, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Core neurons are not selective for different song types at the onset of sensorimotor learning.
source: In contrast, core neurons are not selective for different song types at the onset of sensorimotor learning, but gradually become selectively tuned to playback of their own song (Doupe, 1997; Solis and Doupe, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies of core neuron responses.

claim: Core neurons gradually become selectively tuned to playback of their own song.
source: In contrast, core neurons are not selective for different song types at the onset of sensorimotor learning, but gradually become selectively tuned to playback of their own song (Doupe, 1997; Solis and Doupe, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing developmental changes in core neuron selectivity.

claim: Core neurons that project to vocal motor cortex (RA) send transient axon collaterals into the shell pathway only in juvenile birds.
source: In addition, core neurons that project to vocal motor cortex (RA, Figure 1) send transient axon collaterals into the shell pathway, such that a copy of the motor signal is conveyed into the shell circuit only in juvenile birds (Miller-Sims and Bottjer, 2012) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an anatomical study and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The large population of tutor-tuned neurons in LMAN-shell is gone by late stages of sensorimotor learning.
source: Remarkably, the large population of tutor-tuned neurons in LMAN-shell is gone by late stages of sensorimotor learning, suggesting a key role for this subpopulation during a restricted period of development.
evidence: This is based on observations of developmental changes in the incidence of tutor-tuned neurons.

claim: The shell pathway may evaluate feedback about current vocal performance in relation to a memory of the tutor song during early sensorimotor learning and transmit that evaluation to core and other motor pathways.
source: These developmental changes suggest that the shell pathway may evaluate feedback about current vocal performance in relation to a memory of the tutor song during early sensorimotor learning and transmit that evaluation to core and other motor pathways (Achiro and Bottjer, 2013; Bottjer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from developmental changes and supported by citations.

claim: The majority of neurons in both core and shell showed significant modulation of firing rate during singing.
source: The majority of neurons in both core and shell showed significant modulation of firing rate during singing (Table 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: Among neurons that exhibited a significant change in firing rate during song production, approximately 65–70% showed excitation in both core and shell whereas the remainder were suppressed.
source: Among neurons that exhibited a significant change in firing rate during song production, approximately 65–70% showed excitation in both core and shell whereas the remainder were suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on the proportions of excited and suppressed neurons.

claim: Excitatory response strength was marginally higher in shell neurons.
source: Excitatory response strength was marginally higher in shell neurons, whereas suppressed response strength did not differ between core and shell (Table 1; Mann-Whitney tests: singing-excited neurons U = 1768, p=0.06, singing-suppressed neurons U = 459, p=0.90).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of response strengths between core and shell.

claim: Suppressed response strength did not differ between core and shell.
source: Excitatory response strength was marginally higher in shell neurons, whereas suppressed response strength did not differ between core and shell (Table 1; Mann-Whitney tests: singing-excited neurons U = 1768, p=0.06, singing-suppressed neurons U = 459, p=0.90).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison showing no significant difference.

claim: Singing-excited neurons in both core and shell showed a significant increase in bursting during singing.
source: Singing-excited neurons in both core and shell showed a significant increase in bursting during singing (fraction of spikes with interspike intervals <10 ms; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) as shown previously for LMAN-core neurons in juvenile birds (Olveczky et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: Firing rates of neurons in core and shell were similar during production of different syllable types and lacked temporal specificity across renditions of the same syllable type.
source: Firing rates of neurons in core and shell were also similar during production of different syllable types and lacked temporal specificity across renditions of the same syllable type (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spiking was relatively sparse and variable within and across syllable types in both core and shell neurons.
source: Thus, spiking was relatively sparse and variable within and across syllable types in both core and shell neurons, as reported previously in core for both juvenile and adult birds during playback and singing (Doupe, 1997; Doupe and Solis, 1997; Kao et al., 2008; Olveczky et al., 2005; Solis and Doupe, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: The basic profile of neural activity during song production was similar between shell and core neurons.
source: In summary, the basic profile of neural activity during song production was similar between shell and core neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Population histograms of mean-subtracted responses in pre-singing excited neurons showed synchronous increases in firing rates prior to syllable onsets in core neurons.
source: In accord with this idea, population histograms of mean-subtracted responses in pre-singing excited neurons showed synchronous increases in firing rates prior to syllable onsets in core neurons, whereas shell neurons revealed no evidence for coordinated pre-singing increases in firing rate (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Shell neurons revealed no evidence for coordinated pre-singing increases in firing rate.
source: In accord with this idea, population histograms of mean-subtracted responses in pre-singing excited neurons showed synchronous increases in firing rates prior to syllable onsets in core neurons, whereas shell neurons revealed no evidence for coordinated pre-singing increases in firing rate (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The lack of time-locked premotor activity in shell neurons is consistent with the absence of motor abnormalities following lesions that disrupt shell circuitry.
source: The lack of time-locked premotor activity in shell neurons is consistent with the absence of motor abnormalities following lesions that disrupt shell circuitry (Bottjer and Altenau, 2010), indicating a non-motor role in learning.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the neural activity pattern to lesion data from a cited study.

claim: A large proportion of shell neurons are specifically tuned to playback of either the tutor song or the current version of self-generated song during early stages of sensorimotor integration.
source: A large proportion of shell neurons are specifically tuned to playback of either the tutor song or the current version of self-generated song during early stages of sensorimotor integration when core neurons drive vocal motor output and lesions of LMAN pathways cause disruption of song learning (Achiro and Bottjer, 2013; Aronov et al., 2008; Bottjer et al., 1984; Olveczky et al., 2005; Scharff and Nottebohm, 1991; Bottjer and Altenau, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Firing rates of cells in both core and shell could either increase or decrease as a function of tutor similarity.
source: Unexpectedly, this analysis revealed that firing rates of cells in both core and shell could either increase or decrease as a function of tutor similarity: approximately half of all neurons in each subregion showed increased firing rates for syllables with higher tutor similarity (positive slopes, r values > 0), whereas the other half showed increased firing rates for syllables with lower tutor similarity (negative slopes, r values < 0) (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Table 2.

claim: Approximately half of all neurons in each subregion showed increased firing rates for syllables with higher tutor similarity (positive slopes), whereas the other half showed increased firing rates for syllables with lower tutor similarity (negative slopes).
source: Unexpectedly, this analysis revealed that firing rates of cells in both core and shell could either increase or decrease as a function of tutor similarity: approximately half of all neurons in each subregion showed increased firing rates for syllables with higher tutor similarity (positive slopes, r values > 0), whereas the other half showed increased firing rates for syllables with lower tutor similarity (negative slopes, r values < 0) (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Table 2.

claim: LMAN neurons can encode similarity between self-generated utterances and tutor song via either increases or decreases in firing rate.
source: Thus, LMAN neurons can encode similarity between self-generated utterances and tutor song via either increases or decreases in firing rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing both positive and negative correlations.

claim: The percent of significant neurons compared to random distributions was 5.5% in core and 10.8% in shell.
source: The percent of significant neurons compared to these random distributions was 5.5% in core and 10.8% in shell (Table 2) (chi-square test between core and shell proportions = 1.98, p=0.18).
evidence: This is supported by permutation test analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Tutor similarity predicted the firing rates of a relatively small percentage of single neurons in both core and shell, with somewhat more neurons in shell showing a significant correlation.
source: In summary, tutor similarity predicted the firing rates of a relatively small percentage of single neurons in both core and shell, with somewhat more neurons in shell showing a significant correlation.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical analysis of single neuron correlations.

claim: Mixed-effects linear regression analysis yielded a significant effect for shell neurons but not for core neurons.
source: This analysis yielded a significant effect for shell neurons (t = −2.23, p=0.035) but not for core neurons (t = 0.91,p=0.37), indicating that the population activity of shell neurons during singing reflected tutor-matching performance.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of population-level data.

claim: The population activity of shell neurons during singing reflected tutor-matching performance.
source: This analysis yielded a significant effect for shell neurons (t = −2.23, p=0.035) but not for core neurons (t = 0.91,p=0.37), indicating that the population activity of shell neurons during singing reflected tutor-matching performance.
evidence: This is inferred from the significant statistical effect in the mixed-effects model.

claim: Using the mixed-effects linear regression model, significant effects were found for positive and negative relationships between firing rate and tutor similarity in both core and shell neurons.
source: Using the mixed-effects linear regression model to provide a descriptive assessment of the magnitude of positive and negative associations, we found significant effects for positive and negative relationships between firing rate and tutor similarity in both core and shell neurons (core positive: t = 3.42, p=0.003; negative: t = −2.90, p=0.004; shell positive: t = 4.02, p=0.001; negative: t = −2.80, p=0.009).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data separated by positive and negative slopes.

claim: The majority of neurons in both core and shell showed either higher or lower firing rates during production of syllables with higher tutor similarity.
source: These data indicate that the majority of neurons in both core and shell showed either higher or lower firing rates during production of syllables with higher tutor similarity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the response strength data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The significant association between firing rate and tutor similarity in shell neurons does not reflect a tendency to encode highly prototypical syllables.
source: We tested whether the significant correlation to tutor similarity we observed in shell neurons reflected a tendency to encode highly prototypical syllables using the mixed-effects regression model described above. This analysis showed a non-significant effect (t = −1.53, p=0.136), and there was no relationship between indices of tutor similarity and prototypicality (data not shown), indicating that tutor-similar syllable renditions are not more prototypical.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect of prototypicality.

claim: The relationship between firing rates and tutor similarity in shell neurons does not appear to be based on prototypicality of self-generated syllables.
source: Thus, the relationship between firing rates and tutor similarity in shell neurons does not appear to be based on prototypicality of self-generated syllables.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the prototypicality analysis.

claim: Both core and shell neurons showed increased firing rate variability during production of syllable utterances with low tutor similarity compared to those with high similarity.
source: Both core and shell neurons showed increased firing rate variability during production of syllable utterances with low tutor similarity compared to those with high similarity (Figure 6A; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, core Z = −5.70, p<0.001; shell Z = −4.48, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of CV data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Variability of firing rates during singing reflected the degree of tutor song matching in both core and shell neurons such that responses were less variable for syllable renditions that were more similar to tutor song.
source: Thus, variability of firing rates during singing reflected the degree of tutor song matching in both core and shell neurons such that responses were less variable for syllable renditions that were more similar to tutor song.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CV analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the fraction of syllable types represented in high- versus low-similarity categories.
source: To test this idea, we assessed the fraction of syllable types (across all syllable renditions) that were produced within the high- versus low-similarity categories for each day of singing and found no significant difference (Figure 6B left; Mann-Whitney U = 693, p=0.06).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of syllable type distributions.

claim: There was no difference in the scatter of syllable renditions within a syllable type between the high- and low-similarity to tutor categories.
source: In addition, there was no difference in the scatter of syllable renditions within a syllable type between the high- and low-similarity to tutor categories (Figure 6B right; Mann-Whitney U = 867.5, p=0.90).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of syllable scatter.

claim: Variability in firing rate was higher across the populations of both core and shell neurons during production of syllable renditions with low tutor similarity compared to production of syllable renditions with high tutor similarity.
source: In summary, these data indicate that variability in firing rate was higher across the populations of both core and shell neurons during production of syllable renditions with low tutor similarity compared to production of syllable renditions with high tutor similarity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the CV analysis.

claim: The developmental span over which birds were recorded (43–60 dph) corresponds with a transition from highly variable 'subsong' to 'plastic song' with less behavioral variability and a corresponding increase in similarity to tutor song.
source: The developmental span over which we recorded birds' vocal behavior (43–60 dph) corresponds with a transition from highly variable 'subsong' to 'plastic song' with less behavioral variability and a corresponding increase in similarity to tutor song.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of songbird vocal development.

claim: Comparing degree of song development with acoustic similarity to tutor across average syllable types yielded a significant correlation.
source: Comparing degree of song development with acoustic similarity to tutor across average syllable types yielded a significant correlation (Figure 7A; r = 0.23, p=0.03), supporting the canonical understanding that juvenile birds produce syllable renditions that are more similar to tutor syllables as sensorimotor integration progresses.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of developmental and acoustic data.

claim: Juvenile birds produce syllable renditions that are more similar to tutor syllables as sensorimotor integration progresses.
source: Comparing degree of song development with acoustic similarity to tutor across average syllable types yielded a significant correlation (Figure 7A; r = 0.23, p=0.03), supporting the canonical understanding that juvenile birds produce syllable renditions that are more similar to tutor syllables as sensorimotor integration progresses.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the current data.

claim: Birds produced many utterances with relatively high tutor similarity during subsong.
source: Surprisingly, we found that birds produced many utterances with relatively high tutor similarity during subsong (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The level of tutor matching among high-similarity utterances was fairly constant across development such that there was no significant correlation between tutor similarity and song development.
source: Furthermore, the level of tutor matching among these utterances was fairly constant across development such that there was no significant correlation between tutor similarity and song development (r = 0.13, p=0.42).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationship.

claim: Some of the highly variable vocalizations produced by birds during early sensorimotor learning are good matches to tutor syllables.
source: This striking finding indicates that some of the highly variable vocalizations produced by birds during early sensorimotor learning are good matches to tutor syllables.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on high-similarity utterances in subsong.

claim: The similarity between poorly-matched renditions and tutor syllables increased as song development progressed.
source: Birds in subsong also produced many low-similarity utterances (Figure 7B, left), and the similarity between these poorly-matched renditions and tutor syllables increased as song development progressed, reflecting the expected increase in tutor matching (r = 0.34, p=0.03; cf. Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of low-similarity utterances across development.

claim: Birds in subsong produce some utterances with tutor similarity as high as that of birds in later stages of song development, and renditions with lower tutor similarity at the beginning of sensorimotor integration are gradually eliminated.
source: Thus, birds in subsong produce some utterances with tutor similarity as high as that of birds in later stages of song development, and renditions with lower tutor similarity at the beginning of sensorimotor integration are gradually eliminated.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the developmental analysis of tutor similarity.

claim: The syllable type that was produced most frequently in the high-similarity category was also produced most frequently in the low-similarity category in 57% of vocal recording sessions across all birds.
source: We examined whether individual syllable types were selectively represented in high- versus low-similarity categories for each day of singing, and found that the syllable type that was produced most frequently in the high-similarity category (highest percentage of renditions among all syllable types) was also produced most frequently in the low-similarity category. The most common syllable type produced was the same for both high- and low-similarity renditions in 57% of vocal recording sessions across all birds, indicating that a single syllable type did not typically predominate in either low- or high- similarity categories.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of syllable type distributions in high- and low-similarity categories.

claim: Syllable renditions within both high- and low-similarity categories represent multiple syllable types.
source: This pattern is consistent with the finding above that syllable renditions within both high- and low-similarity categories represent multiple syllable types (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a conclusion consistent with previous analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Absolute values of response strength across song development increased in both core and shell neurons regardless of whether syllable renditions had high or low similarity to tutor syllables.
source: Absolute values of response strength across song development increased in both core and shell neurons regardless of whether syllable renditions had high or low similarity to tutor syllables (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: This pattern agrees with previously published work showing increases in firing rate of RA neurons as song learning progresses.
source: This pattern agrees with previously published work showing increases in firing rate of RA neurons as song learning progresses (Ölveczky et al., 2011), suggesting generic increases in firing rate with development.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study showing similar developmental increases.

claim: LMAN circuitry is critical for early sensorimotor learning when the number of tutor-tuned shell neurons is high.
source: However, LMAN circuitry is critical for early sensorimotor learning when the number of tutor-tuned shell neurons is high (Achiro and Bottjer, 2013), indicating that the involvement of LMAN may be high initially when the goal representation is strong and decrease as learning progresses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and inference about the role of LMAN.

claim: Both core and shell neurons showed stronger associations between firing rate and tutor similarity during early stages of song development, and weaker associations as sensorimotor learning progressed.
source: Both core and shell neurons showed stronger associations between firing rate and tutor similarity during early stages of song development, and weaker associations as sensorimotor learning progressed.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis across development shown in Figure 8.

claim: The activity of both core and shell neurons reflects the degree of song learning: tutor similarity is a better predictor of firing rate during early sensorimotor learning when many utterances have low tutor similarity, and the strength of this association decreases in parallel with developmental increases in motor performance as song learning progresses.
source: This pattern indicates that the activity of both core and shell neurons reflects the degree of song learning: tutor similarity is a better predictor of firing rate during early sensorimotor learning when many utterances have low tutor similarity (Figure 7B), and the strength of this association decreases in parallel with developmental increases in motor performance as song learning progresses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the developmental analysis of correlations between firing rate and tutor similarity.

claim: CV of firing rate in shell neurons decreased over the course of song development only during production of syllable renditions that had low similarity to tutor during early sensorimotor learning.
source: CV of firing rate in shell neurons decreased over the course of song development only during production of syllable renditions that had low similarity to tutor during early sensorimotor learning (Figure 9; low similarity, r = −0.24,p=0.01; high similarity, r = −0.08, p=0.42).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of CV across development shown in Figure 9.

claim: Variability of firing in shell neurons did not change for utterances with high similarity to tutor song across development.
source: Thus, variability of firing in shell neurons did not change for utterances with high similarity to tutor song across development.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the CV analysis showing no significant correlation for high-similarity utterances.

claim: The CV of firing rate in core neurons did not change as a function of song development regardless of whether syllable renditions had high or low tutor similarity.
source: In contrast, the CV of firing rate in core neurons did not change as a function of song development regardless of whether syllable renditions had high or low tutor similarity (Figure 9; low similarity,r = 0.04, p=0.73; high similarity, r = 0.05, p=0.61).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationships.

claim: The variability of firing in shell neurons reflected the progression of learning, with higher neural variability early in development for renditions with lower similarity to tutor song, and lower neural variability later in development as the incidence of poorly-matched syllable renditions decreased.
source: These data show that the variability of firing in shell neurons reflected the progression of learning, with higher neural variability early in development for renditions with lower similarity to tutor song, and lower neural variability later in development as the incidence of poorly-matched syllable renditions decreased.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the developmental CV analysis.

claim: Neurons in both core and shell subregions of LMAN showed singing-related activity that varied as a function of tutor song similarity during early stages of sensorimotor integration.
source: We tested whether spiking activity in LMAN of juvenile birds reflects the acoustic similarity of self-generated vocal utterances to memorized tutor syllables. Neurons in both core and shell subregions of LMAN showed singing-related activity that varied as a function of tutor song similarity during early stages of sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: This pattern represents the first discovery of an online correlate of song performance during learning in juvenile birds.
source: This pattern represents the first discovery of an online correlate of song performance during learning in juvenile birds and suggests LMAN as a key component of circuitry that evaluates current behavior in relation to a goal behavior during procedural learning.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: LMAN is a key component of circuitry that evaluates current behavior in relation to a goal behavior during procedural learning.
source: This pattern represents the first discovery of an online correlate of song performance during learning in juvenile birds and suggests LMAN as a key component of circuitry that evaluates current behavior in relation to a goal behavior during procedural learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing neural encoding of tutor similarity.

claim: Although neural activity across the population in both core and shell was modulated by degree of similarity between self-generated sounds and memorized tutor sounds, this trend was stronger across the population of shell neurons.
source: Although neural activity across the population in both core and shell was modulated by degree of similarity between self-generated sounds and memorized tutor sounds, this trend was stronger across the population of shell neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the population-level statistical findings.

claim: Spiking activity in core neurons supports the idea that core drives vocal motor output in juvenile birds.
source: As in prior work, we found that spiking activity in core neurons supports the idea that core drives vocal motor output in juvenile birds (Aronov et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and citation to previous work.

claim: Neural activity in shell neurons did not exhibit coordinated premotor increases in firing rate.
source: In contrast, neural activity in shell neurons did not exhibit coordinated premotor increases in firing rate, which is consistent with the lack of projections from shell to downstream motor circuitry and the absence of motor disruption following lesions to the shell pathway (Bottjer and Altenau, 2010; Bottjer et al., 2000) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous anatomical and lesion studies.

claim: Shell circuitry acts primarily as a 'critic' to evaluate comparisons between self-generated and tutor sounds, while core circuitry serves as an 'actor' that drives vocal motor output and receives instruction from the critic in order to bias action selection over the course of learning.
source: One interpretation of this pattern of results is that shell circuitry acts primarily as a 'critic' to evaluate comparisons between self-generated and tutor sounds, while core circuitry serves as an 'actor' that drives vocal motor output and receives instruction from the critic in order to bias action selection over the course of learning (Barto et al., 1983; Graybiel, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results, supported by citations to actor-critic models.

claim: Some individual syllable renditions were similar to tutor syllables even in subsong birds during early sensorimotor integration, indicating a surprising capacity to produce relatively mature syllabic utterances.
source: Interestingly, some individual syllable renditions were similar to tutor syllables even in subsong birds during early sensorimotor integration, indicating a surprising capacity to produce relatively mature syllabic utterances.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data on tutor similarity in subsong.

claim: This result is reminiscent of the finding that juvenile birds exposed to adult females are able to produce more stereotyped song patterns than normally seen in young birds.
source: This result is reminiscent of the finding that juvenile birds exposed to adult females are able to produce more stereotyped song patterns than normally seen in young birds (Kojima and Doupe, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to a previous finding, supported by citation.

claim: The ability to produce syllable renditions that represent a range of matches to the goal (i.e. both higher and lower similarity) may be an important component of the behavioral variability that is necessary for skill acquisition involving reinforcement learning.
source: The ability to produce syllable renditions that represent a range of matches to the goal (i.e. both higher and lower similarity) may be an important component of the behavioral variability that is necessary for skill acquisition involving reinforcement learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the functional significance of the behavioral findings.

claim: Only syllable utterances with low levels of tutor matching during subsong showed a progressive increase in tutor similarity over the course of development.
source: Only syllable utterances with low levels of tutor matching during subsong showed a progressive increase in tutor similarity over the course of development, and the activity of shell but not core neurons reflected this difference in behavioral trajectory.
evidence: This is supported by the developmental analysis of tutor similarity.

claim: The activity of shell but not core neurons reflected the difference in behavioral trajectory between high- and low-similarity utterances across development.
source: Only syllable utterances with low levels of tutor matching during subsong showed a progressive increase in tutor similarity over the course of development, and the activity of shell but not core neurons reflected this difference in behavioral trajectory.
evidence: This is supported by the CV analysis showing developmental changes only in shell neurons.

claim: Developmental changes in firing rate variability mirrored that seen for behavioral development only in shell.
source: Developmental changes in firing rate variability mirrored that seen for behavioral development only in shell (Figures 7 and 9): firing rate CV in shell neurons decreased throughout development only among utterances that showed an increase in similarity over the course of learning.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of behavioral and neural developmental trajectories.

claim: Variability of firing in core neurons did not change developmentally.
source: In contrast, variability of firing in core neurons did not change developmentally.
evidence: This is supported by the CV analysis showing no developmental changes in core.

claim: The decrease in variable firing in shell neurons in parallel with the decrease in incidence of poorly matched syllable renditions indicates that the activity of shell neurons tracks the degree of song matching.
source: The decrease in variable firing in shell neurons in parallel with the decrease in incidence of poorly matched syllable renditions indicates that the activity of shell neurons tracks the degree of song matching, consistent with the hypothesis that these neurons are involved in comparing song behavior to a tutor song memory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parallel developmental changes in behavior and neural activity.

claim: As vocal behavior was refined to achieve a more accurate imitation of tutor song, the correlation between tutor similarity and firing rate decreased in both core and shell neurons.
source: As vocal behavior was refined to achieve a more accurate imitation of tutor song, the correlation between tutor similarity and firing rate decreased in both core and shell neurons (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the developmental analysis of correlations shown in Figure 8.

claim: The tendency toward weaker encoding of tutor similarity by firing rate as song learning progresses coincides with the loss of a large population of shell neurons that respond selectively to playback of tutor song.
source: The tendency toward weaker encoding of tutor similarity by firing rate as song learning progresses coincides with the loss of a large population of shell neurons that respond selectively to playback of tutor song (Achiro and Bottjer, 2013).
evidence: This connects the current findings to previous observations about tutor-tuned neurons, supported by citation.

claim: Tutor similarity is a better predictor of firing rate during early learning when behavioral variability is high and shell contains a large population of tutor-selective neurons.
source: Thus, tutor similarity is a better predictor of firing rate during early learning when behavioral variability is high and shell contains a large population of tutor-selective neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating multiple findings.

claim: The loss of tutor-tuned neurons along with a progressive weakening of the association between firing rate and tutor similarity suggests that birds may be switching to a different strategy such as comparing their own utterances to a 'self' template more than to a tutor template.
source: The loss of tutor-tuned neurons along with a progressive weakening of the association between firing rate and tutor similarity suggests that birds may be switching to a different strategy such as comparing their own utterances to a 'self' template more than to a tutor template.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the developmental changes.

claim: Neural selectivity for self-generated sounds increases in core neurons between 45 and 60 dph.
source: In accord with this idea, neural selectivity for self-generated sounds increases in core neurons between 45 and 60 dph (Achiro and Bottjer, 2013; Doupe, 1997; Doupe and Solis, 1997; Solis and Doupe, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing developmental changes in selectivity.

claim: Tutor-tuned neurons in juvenile LMAN-shell may act as a gate or filter for self-generated utterances that are tutor-similar.
source: Tutor-tuned neurons in juvenile LMAN-shell may act as a gate or filter for self-generated utterances that are tutor-similar, suggesting that evaluation of tutor similarity within LMAN may be selectively vested in the firing rate of neurons within this subtype during early sensorimotor integration.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the function of tutor-tuned neurons.

claim: Increases in firing rates for syllables with higher tutor similarity (positive slopes) could provide a reinforcement signal to increase the probability of producing that vocal pattern.
source: One possibility is that increases in firing rates for syllables with higher tutor similarity (positive slopes) could provide a reinforcement signal to increase the probability of producing that vocal pattern, whereas increases in firing rates for syllables with lower tutor similarity (negative slopes) could provide an error signal to decrease the probability of making that incorrect sound; both types of information could be conveyed to downstream neurons and used to guide accurate refinement of syllables during learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of positive and negative correlations.

claim: Increases in firing rates for syllables with lower tutor similarity (negative slopes) could provide an error signal to decrease the probability of making that incorrect sound.
source: One possibility is that increases in firing rates for syllables with higher tutor similarity (positive slopes) could provide a reinforcement signal to increase the probability of producing that vocal pattern, whereas increases in firing rates for syllables with lower tutor similarity (negative slopes) could provide an error signal to decrease the probability of making that incorrect sound; both types of information could be conveyed to downstream neurons and used to guide accurate refinement of syllables during learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of positive and negative correlations.

claim: Both types of information (reinforcement and error signals) could be conveyed to downstream neurons and used to guide accurate refinement of syllables during learning.
source: One possibility is that increases in firing rates for syllables with higher tutor similarity (positive slopes) could provide a reinforcement signal to increase the probability of producing that vocal pattern, whereas increases in firing rates for syllables with lower tutor similarity (negative slopes) could provide an error signal to decrease the probability of making that incorrect sound; both types of information could be conveyed to downstream neurons and used to guide accurate refinement of syllables during learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about how the neural signals might guide learning.

claim: The involvement of LMAN circuitry in goal-oriented learning is likely to be strongly dependent on developmental changes that occur in these pathways.
source: The involvement of LMAN circuitry in goal-oriented learning is likely to be strongly dependent on developmental changes that occur in these pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental changes observed and discussed.

claim: In juveniles, but not adults, many core neurons that project to vocal motor cortex send a collateral branch into the shell pathway.
source: In juveniles, but not adults, many core neurons that project to vocal motor cortex send a collateral branch into the shell pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) (Miller-Sims and Bottjer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an anatomical study and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: This transient pathway may transmit a copy of the premotor signal generated by core neurons to shell neurons.
source: This transient pathway may transmit a copy of the premotor signal generated by core neurons to shell neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of the transient projection.

claim: The incidence of shell neurons tuned to learned tutor sounds decreases sharply during development.
source: In addition, the incidence of shell neurons tuned to learned tutor sounds decreases sharply (Achiro and Bottjer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Because the overall volume of shell regresses sharply during development, it may be that tutor-tuned neurons are eliminated due to naturally-occurring cell death, thereby helping to close the sensitive period for learning.
source: Because the overall volume of shell regresses sharply during development, it may be that tutor-tuned neurons are eliminated due to naturally-occurring cell death (Johnson and Bottjer, 1992; Johnson et al., 1995), thereby helping to close the sensitive period for learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to studies of cell death.

claim: Topographic specificity develops in the projection from LMAN core to RA (vocal motor cortex) during early development and is dependent on normal auditory experience.
source: Topographic specificity develops in the projection from LMAN core to RA (vocal motor cortex) during early development and is dependent on normal auditory experience (Iyengar and Bottjer, 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A high proportion of synapses formed by thalamic axons in LMAN are 'silent synapses' in early development.
source: In addition, a high proportion of synapses formed by thalamic axons in LMAN are 'silent synapses' in early development (Bottjer, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A decrease in the number of silent synapses may contribute to a period of synaptic refinement to confer greater specificity of connectivity in thalamo-cortical connections as well as to curtail the sensitive period.
source: a decrease in their number may contribute to a period of synaptic refinement to confer greater specificity of connectivity in thalamo-cortical connections (Iyengar and Bottjer, 2002a; Nixdorf-Bergweiler, 2001); cf. Garst-Orozco et al., 2014) as well as to curtail the sensitive period (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: These developmental changes suggest that differences in the extent and plasticity of neural mechanisms may be causally related to goal-oriented learning during development, and help to explain decreases in behavioral plasticity in older animals.
source: These developmental changes suggest that differences in the extent and plasticity of neural mechanisms may be causally related to goal-oriented learning during development, and help to explain decreases in behavioral plasticity in older animals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the functional significance of developmental changes.

claim: A functional segregation of vocal learning into parallel core and shell cortico-basal ganglia loops is reminiscent of corresponding architecture in sensorimotor and associative cortico-basal ganglia loops of mammals.
source: A functional segregation of vocal learning into parallel core and shell cortico-basal ganglia loops is reminiscent of corresponding architecture in sensorimotor and associative cortico-basal ganglia loops of mammals.
evidence: This is a comparative inference about the similarity between songbird and mammalian circuits.

claim: Studies in mammals have shown that neurons in associative loops show increased modulation early in learning of goal-directed tasks, whereas sensorimotor circuits increase their activity throughout training and may encode learned motor performance.
source: Studies in mammals have shown that neurons in associative loops show increased modulation early in learning of goal-directed tasks, whereas sensorimotor circuits increase their activity throughout training and may encode learned motor performance (Joel and Weiner, 1997; Histed et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2009; Thorn et al., 2010; Gremel and Costa, 2013; Kim et al., 2013; Samejima and Doya, 2007; Graybiel, 2008; Yin et al., 2008; Ashby et al., 2010; Redgrave et al., 2010; Ito and Doya, 2015; Lehéricy et al., 2005; Thorn and Graybiel, 2014; Atallah et al., 2007; Nakahara et al., 2001; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to mammalian studies.

claim: Evidence has suggested that associative loops function to evaluate motor performance during early stages of learning and sensorimotor loops encode behaviors as they become more habitual.
source: Such evidence has suggested that associative loops function to evaluate motor performance during early stages of learning and sensorimotor loops encode behaviors as they become more habitual (Makino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review or study of mammalian circuits.

claim: The overall patterns of neural activity observed in shell and core are consistent with recent data showing that both associative and sensorimotor cortico-striatal circuits are engaged in skill acquisition, but that associative circuits disengage early in learning whereas sensorimotor circuits remain engaged.
source: The overall patterns of neural activity we observed in shell and core are consistent with recent data showing that both associative and sensorimotor cortico-striatal circuits are engaged in skill acquisition, but that associative circuits disengage early in learning whereas sensorimotor circuits remain engaged (Kupferschmidt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to recent mammalian data, supported by citation.

claim: The decline in spiking variability in shell neurons is consistent with a decreased involvement of associative circuits during early skill acquisition.
source: The decline in spiking variability in shell neurons is consistent with a decreased involvement of associative circuits during early skill acquisition (Thorn et al., 2010; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the shell neuron data in the context of mammalian studies, supported by citations.

claim: Although variability of firing rate did not change developmentally in core neurons, firing rate CV was higher for syllable renditions with low tutor similarity in core neurons when averaged across all ages.
source: In addition, although variability of firing rate did not change developmentally in core neurons, firing rate CV was higher for syllable renditions with low tutor similarity in core neurons when averaged across all ages (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the CV data shown in Figure 6.

claim: This pattern suggests that core neurons may retain an exploratory (variable) mode, maintaining a higher CV for poorly-matched syllable renditions and a lower CV for well-matched renditions.
source: This pattern suggests that core neurons may retain an exploratory (variable) mode (Graybiel, 2005), maintaining a higher CV for poorly-matched syllable renditions and a lower CV for well-matched renditions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the core neuron CV data, with citation to a relevant concept.

claim: Such an outcome would be consistent with the idea that core neurons retain some level of engagement at later stages of sensorimotor learning.
source: Such an outcome would be consistent with the idea that core neurons retain some level of engagement at later stages of sensorimotor learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the continued role of core neurons.

claim: The present results support the idea that motor learning across taxa entails the integrative product of multiple circuits whose functions reflect specific aspects during the progression of learning.
source: Overall, the present results support the idea that motor learning across taxa entails the integrative product of multiple circuits whose functions reflect specific aspects during the progression of learning.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion drawn from the current findings in the context of comparative neuroscience.

claim: Ten juvenile male zebra finches were used, 43–60 days post hatch at the time of neural recordings.
source: Ten juvenile male zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) were used, 43–60 days post hatch (dph) at the time of neural recordings
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The period of sensorimotor integration begins in zebra finches when young males produce variable babbling sounds (subsong) starting at approximately 35 dph, and continues until the birds begin to produce a stereotyped imitation of the tutor song around 70–90 dph.
source: The period of sensorimotor integration begins in zebra finches when young males produce variable babbling sounds (subsong) starting at approximately 35 dph, and continues until the birds begin to produce a stereotyped imitation of the tutor song around 70–90 dph.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebra finch vocal development.

claim: Birds were raised under naturalistic conditions (by their parents within group aviaries) until they were at least 38 dph, ensuring normal tutor song exposure and social experience.
source: Birds were raised under naturalistic conditions (by their parents within group aviaries) until they were at least 38 dph, ensuring normal tutor song exposure and social experience (Böhner, 1990; Immelmann, 1969; Roper and Zann, 2006; Böhner, 1983; Eales, 1985; Clayton, 1987; Mann and Slater, 1995; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, supported by citations to studies on rearing conditions.

claim: Calbindin expression specifically labels thalamic axons terminating in LMAN.
source: calbindin expression specifically labels thalamic axons terminating in LMAN (Pinaud et al., 2007; Achiro and Bottjer, 2013) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The border between core and shell subregions of LMAN can be distinguished based on the density of magnocellular somata.
source: The border between core and shell subregions of LMAN can be distinguished based on the density of magnocellular somata, and the outer borders of shell can be distinguished from surrounding regions based on the limit of calbindin expression (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of anatomical criteria used to define regions, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The outer borders of shell can be distinguished from surrounding regions based on the limit of calbindin expression.
source: The border between core and shell subregions of LMAN can be distinguished based on the density of magnocellular somata, and the outer borders of shell can be distinguished from surrounding regions based on the limit of calbindin expression (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of anatomical criteria used to define regions, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bilateral lesion of AId as juveniles prevents imitation of the tutor song as well as the development of a stereotyped sequence of syllables.
source: Lesions of AId prevent imitation of the tutor song as well as the development of a stereotyped sequence of syllables; however, the phonology of syllables is normal, indicating that AId lesions do not exert an effect on vocal motor production.
evidence: This is supported by lesion data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phonology of syllables is normal following AId lesions, indicating that AId lesions do not exert an effect on vocal motor production.
source: Lesions of AId prevent imitation of the tutor song as well as the development of a stereotyped sequence of syllables; however, the phonology of syllables is normal, indicating that AId lesions do not exert an effect on vocal motor production.
evidence: This is an inference from the lesion data showing selective impairment of learning but not motor production.

claim: Individual core neurons show significant responses to playback of their own song only or to both their own song and the tutor song.
source: Individual core neurons show significant responses to playback of their own song only or to both their own song and the tutor song (and frequently to other songs as well, data not shown); few core neurons respond to tutor song only.
evidence: This is supported by playback response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Few core neurons respond to tutor song only.
source: Individual core neurons show significant responses to playback of their own song only or to both their own song and the tutor song (and frequently to other songs as well, data not shown); few core neurons respond to tutor song only.
evidence: This is supported by playback response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Individual shell neurons show significant responses either to their own song or to tutor song.
source: In contrast, individual shell neurons show significant responses either to their own song or to tutor song; few shell neurons respond to playback of both their own song and tutor song.
evidence: This is supported by playback response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Few shell neurons respond to playback of both their own song and tutor song.
source: In contrast, individual shell neurons show significant responses either to their own song or to tutor song; few shell neurons respond to playback of both their own song and tutor song.
evidence: This is supported by playback response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A large population of shell neurons (~30%) responds significantly to tutor song, but not to own song (or other control songs).
source: Thus, a large population of shell neurons (~30%) responds significantly to tutor song, but not to own song (or other control songs).
evidence: This is supported by playback response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: LMAN contains representations of both current behavior (self-generated song) and the goal behavior (tutor song).
source: This pattern indicates that LMAN contains representations of both current behavior (self-generated song) and the goal behavior (tutor song).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of neurons responding to own song and tutor song.

claim: Tutor-tuned neurons are a transient population: their incidence decreases greatly by late stages of sensorimotor integration.
source: Tutor-tuned neurons are a transient population: their incidence decreases greatly by late stages of sensorimotor integration (not shown), indicating that tutor-tuned neurons are eliminated due to cell death or are re-tuned to each bird's own song.
evidence: This is based on observations of developmental changes in tutor-tuned neuron incidence.

claim: Tutor-tuned neurons are eliminated due to cell death or are re-tuned to each bird's own song.
source: Tutor-tuned neurons are a transient population: their incidence decreases greatly by late stages of sensorimotor integration (not shown), indicating that tutor-tuned neurons are eliminated due to cell death or are re-tuned to each bird's own song.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the loss of tutor-tuned neurons.

claim: Many core neurons of juvenile birds, but not adults, extend collaterals into AId.
source: Many core neurons of juvenile birds, but not adults, extend collaterals into AId; in adult birds, core neurons project only to RA and shell neurons project only to AId.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In adult birds, core neurons project only to RA and shell neurons project only to AId.
source: Many core neurons of juvenile birds, but not adults, extend collaterals into AId; in adult birds, core neurons project only to RA and shell neurons project only to AId.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: This transient projection provides a point of integration between the two basal ganglia pathways as juvenile birds are actively engaged in learning but is completely retracted in adult birds.
source: This transient projection provides a point of integration between the two basal ganglia pathways as juvenile birds are actively engaged in learning but is completely retracted in adult birds.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the transient projection.

claim: The transient projection suggests that these branches convey corollary discharge signals, since they are collateral branches of core neurons that drive vocal behavior via RA but lesions of AId do not cause motor disruption.
source: In addition, the transient projection suggests that these branches convey corollary discharge signals, since they are collateral branches of core neurons that drive vocal behavior via RA but lesions of AId do not cause motor disruption.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the function of the transient projection based on anatomical and lesion data.
